p: The two powers began as allies. After Wanyan Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and in 1115 named himself emperor of the Jin, the Song emperor Huizong sought his help against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938. The Jin took the Liao capitals quickly, while Song attacks on Yanjing failed twice in 1122. By the treaty of 1123 the Song received only seven prefectures and agreed to pay the Jin 300,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 taels of silver a year.

The alliance soon broke down. Zhang Jue, a former Liao governor, turned his city over to the Song, though the treaty forbade harbouring defectors, and in 1124 Song officials asked for nine more prefectures. In November 1125 the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack.

Two Jin armies invaded. Kaifeng was first besieged on 31 January 1126, and after 33 days the new emperor Qinzong bought a withdrawal by ceding three prefectures; when he went back on the agreement the Jin returned and broke into the city on 9 January 1127. The Jin then tried to rule the north through puppet states, Da Chu in 1127 and Da Qi from 1130 to 1137. Gaozong, enthroned on 12 June 1127, was pursued as far as the sea in 1130, but the Song navy on the Yangtze and an insurgency in the north checked the invaders.

The peace of 1142 was broken twice. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang invaded in 1161, was defeated at the Battle of Caishi in November and was assassinated by his own officers in December. Under the Song chancellor Han Tuozhou war was declared on 14 June 1206; the offensive failed, and the treaty of 2 November 1208 raised the tribute. Pressed by the Mongols, the Jin attacked the Song again from 1217 until a peace in 1224 ended the tribute. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and in 1234 their troops took Caizhou, where the Jin emperor Aizong killed himself.

Some two to three million Jurchens came to rule about 30 million Han Chinese in the north. Over half a million people fled south in 1126–1127. Lin'an, declared the capital in 1138, grew into a major commercial centre. The wars also spurred gunpowder weapons: the fire lance is first reported at the siege of De'an in 1132, and the iron-cased bombs the Jin used at Qizhou in 1221 are the first known hard-casing bombs. After the Jin fell the Mongols turned on the Song, which collapsed in 1279.

notes: The article writes dates month-first; turned day-first here.

The article says the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack in November 1125; the 1126 siege of Kaifeng began 31 January 1126 and the city fell 9 January 1127 (the 'Jingkang incident' of the description).
Caishi: traditional accounts make it the turning point (18,000 Song against 400,000 Jin); the article says modern analysis finds it a minor battle with about 4,000 Jin casualties. I gave no numbers.
The article names the 1217 Song emperor as Lizong (r. 1224-1264), which cannot be right for 1217; I named no emperor there.
Yue Fei, the Treaty of Shaoxing's border and the captured emperors are in the description and not repeated; the article says Yue Fei was poisoned in jail early in 1142 on Qin Hui's orders.
